sources.title: Toddler Reading Time
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Kandia N. Lewis, PhD, August 2023)
sources.quote: Sitting Still Is Not Required Trying to read to a toddler who won't sit still can be frustrating. Be patient and keep trying. Find a book or a few pages that are interesting. If that doesn't work, don't force the reading but be sure to try again later. Remember that toddlers love repetition — if your child doesn't seem interested in books, you may need to find a favorite and read it over and over again. Some busy toddlers like to stand up while you read to them. Others like to look at a page or two before moving on to something else. Keep the book out — kids might want to return to it later, which you should encourage. It's OK if your child can't sit still for an entire book — toddlers' attention spans will get longer soon.
sources.supports: Sitting still is not required: toddlers may stand, look at a page or two, want the same favorite again and again, attention spans grow soon; if it does not work, try again later and keep the book out.

sources.title: Toddler Reading Time (tips)
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Kandia N. Lewis, PhD, August 2023)
sources.quote: Choosing regular times to read (especially before naps and bedtime) helps kids learn to sit with a book and relax. ... If your toddler will let you, hold them in your lap when you read. This helps your toddler feel safe, happy, and relaxed. ... Encourage this by putting out three or four books and asking your child to pick one. ... Let your toddler help you turn pages ... Read expressively, using different voices for different characters ... Talk about the pictures. Point to items and name them. ... Use your child's name as the name of a character in the book. ... Keep active hands busy with lift-the-flap pages and textures to feel. ... Keep your toddler's interest by choosing books with small amounts of words on the page ... Books about bedtime, baths, or mealtime are all good choices ... Before bedtime, allow your child to touch and play with favorite toys while you read aloud. ... Keep books in a basket on the floor or on a low shelf where your child can reach them
sources.supports: Regular reading times, lap, choosing from three or four books, turning pages, voices, pointing and naming pictures, the child's name as a character, flaps and textures, few words per page, books about daily routines, toys in hand, books kept within reach.

sources.title: Reading with toddlers
sources.publisher: StartingBlocks.gov.au (Australian Government early childhood site, contributed to by Raising Literacy Australia)
sources.quote: Toddlers are learning so much about the world around them that it’s hard to sit still! Don’t worry if you can’t get through a whole book. The main thing to keep in mind when reading with toddlers is that it has more to do with pointing and talking than with them sitting still and listening. ... Be willing to read only parts of a book and pages out of order ... Incorporate movement and actions that go along with the books. For example, when reading 'Humpty Dumpty' pretend to fall with your little one at the right time.
sources.supports: Do not worry about finishing a whole book, read only parts and pages out of order, pointing and talking matter more than sitting still, add movement and actions to the story.

sources.title: Toddler Reading Time (stories)
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Kandia N. Lewis, PhD, August 2023)
sources.quote: Between the ages of 1 and 3, toddlers have celebrations and challenges. So it can help for them to hear stories about other kids and how they faced their fears about what's under the bed or learned how to use the potty.
sources.supports: Hearing stories about other kids facing a challenge can help a toddler. Said as a general help, not a promise of a result.

sources.title: Toddler Reading Time
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Kandia N. Lewis, PhD, August 2023)
sources.quote: Sitting Still Is Not Required Trying to read to a toddler who won't sit still can be frustrating. Be patient and keep trying. Find a book or a few pages that are interesting. If that doesn't work, don't force the reading but be sure to try again later. Remember that toddlers love repetition — if your child doesn't seem interested in books, you may need to find a favorite and read it over and over again. Some busy toddlers like to stand up while you read to them. Others like to look at a page or two before moving on to something else. Keep the book out — kids might want to return to it later, which you should encourage. It's OK if your child can't sit still for an entire book — toddlers' attention spans will get longer soon.
sources.supports: Sitting still is not required: toddlers may stand, look at a page or two, want the same favorite again and again, attention spans grow soon; if it does not work, try again later and keep the book out.

sources.title: Toddler Reading Time (tips)
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Kandia N. Lewis, PhD, August 2023)
sources.quote: Choosing regular times to read (especially before naps and bedtime) helps kids learn to sit with a book and relax. ... If your toddler will let you, hold them in your lap when you read. This helps your toddler feel safe, happy, and relaxed. ... Encourage this by putting out three or four books and asking your child to pick one. ... Let your toddler help you turn pages ... Read expressively, using different voices for different characters ... Talk about the pictures. Point to items and name them. ... Use your child's name as the name of a character in the book. ... Keep active hands busy with lift-the-flap pages and textures to feel. ... Keep your toddler's interest by choosing books with small amounts of words on the page ... Books about bedtime, baths, or mealtime are all good choices ... Before bedtime, allow your child to touch and play with favorite toys while you read aloud. ... Keep books in a basket on the floor or on a low shelf where your child can reach them
sources.supports: Regular reading times, lap, choosing from three or four books, turning pages, voices, pointing and naming pictures, the child's name as a character, flaps and textures, few words per page, books about daily routines, toys in hand, books kept within reach.

sources.title: Reading with toddlers
sources.publisher: StartingBlocks.gov.au (Australian Government early childhood site, contributed to by Raising Literacy Australia)
sources.quote: Toddlers are learning so much about the world around them that it’s hard to sit still! Don’t worry if you can’t get through a whole book. The main thing to keep in mind when reading with toddlers is that it has more to do with pointing and talking than with them sitting still and listening. ... Be willing to read only parts of a book and pages out of order ... Incorporate movement and actions that go along with the books. For example, when reading 'Humpty Dumpty' pretend to fall with your little one at the right time.
sources.supports: Do not worry about finishing a whole book, read only parts and pages out of order, pointing and talking matter more than sitting still, add movement and actions to the story.

sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Kandia N. Lewis, PhD, August 2023)
sources.quote: Between the ages of 1 and 3, toddlers have celebrations and challenges. So it can help for them to hear stories about other kids and how they faced their fears about what's under the bed or learned how to use the potty.
sources.supports: Hearing stories about other kids facing a challenge can help a toddler. Said as a general help, not a promise of a result.

sources.quote: Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. sources.title: When Should Kids Stop Using Pacifiers?
sources.publisher: Cleveland Clinic (pediatrician Jason Sherman, DO, 1 Jan 2026)
sources.quote: “You may have to deal with a few days and nights of fussing,” Dr. Sherman concedes. “But stand firm.” ... Start removing your child’s pacifier when they’re at home, putting it somewhere they can’t see or find it. ... Children suck on pacifiers to self-soothe — and self-soothing is an important skill that helps them sleep. If your child is 1 or older, you can put them to bed with a light blanket or stuffed animal to help soothe them as you try to make the switch away from pacifiers. ... You could, for example, throw a goodbye party for their pacifiers or encourage your child to “trade in” their pacifiers for a new toy they get to pick out on their own. ... Kids are motivated by praise ... be sure to tell them what a great job they’re doing of not using their pacifier. ... If your child is accustomed to using their pacifier to sleep, you’ll want to have a plan in place to help them learn to sleep without it.
sources.supports: A few days and nights of fussing, stand firm, keep it out of sight, self-soothing is a skill, a light blanket or stuffed animal from age 1, a goodbye party or a trade for a toy, praise, and a sleep plan.

עכשיו אני לומד אחרת
הימים הראשונים הכי קשים.
ותעזרו לי עם 8 דברים.

1 תגידו לי מראש
2 קודם רק לשינה
״יונתן עוד יומיים.
נגיד ביי למוצץ״
ובינתיים רק לשינה.

3 דובי או שמיכה קטנה
משהו רך שאני בוחר.
ואני מחבק אותו במקום המוצץ.

4 תורידו אותו מהעיניים
5 תנו אותו לפיית המוצץ
במקום גבוה שאני לא מוצא.
והפיה משאירה לי צעצוע.

6 תהיו איתי
בלילות הקשים
כמה לילות אבכה.
ואתם עדיין לידי.

7 תגידו לי שאני מצליח
״יונתן ישנת בלי מוצץ!״
זה נותן לי כוח להמשיך.

8 תהיו נחושים ועדינים
גם אם אבכה.
תהיו איתי ותישארו עקביים.

דובי, פיה ופרגון
ויד עדינה ונחושה
ככה אני נפרד מהמוצץ.
תעזרו לי בלילות הראשונים?

תשמרו את הפוסט
לפעם הבאה שהוא מחפש את המוצץ בלילה. 🔖

sources.title: Dummies
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health (reviewed 12 Jun 2026)
sources.quote: Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. Tips for removing the dummy Limit the use of the dummy to sleep or nighttime. ... Talk about stopping the dummy for a couple of days to prepare your child. Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. ... Encourage your child to give their dummy away to the dummy fairy, or to another parent of a younger child. Give plenty of encouragement and keep it positive. Persist gently but firmly. The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: Do not stop suddenly, limit it to sleep first, talk about it a couple of days ahead, a chosen cuddly toy in its place, a dummy fairy, encouragement, persist gently but firmly, the first few days are the hardest. Australian state health page, used as general advice.

sources.title: When Should Kids Stop Using Pacifiers?
sources.publisher: Cleveland Clinic (pediatrician Jason Sherman, DO, 1 Jan 2026)
sources.quote: “You may have to deal with a few days and nights of fussing,” Dr. Sherman concedes. “But stand firm.” ... Start removing your child’s pacifier when they’re at home, putting it somewhere they can’t see or find it. ... Children suck on pacifiers to self-soothe — and self-soothing is an important skill that helps them sleep. If your child is 1 or older, you can put them to bed with a light blanket or stuffed animal to help soothe them as you try to make the switch away from pacifiers. ... You could, for example, throw a goodbye party for their pacifiers or encourage your child to “trade in” their pacifiers for a new toy they get to pick out on their own. ... Kids are motivated by praise ... be sure to tell them what a great job they’re doing of not using their pacifier. ... If your child is accustomed to using their pacifier to sleep, you’ll want to have a plan in place to help them learn to sleep without it.
sources.supports: A few days and nights of fussing, stand firm, keep it out of sight, self-soothing is a skill, a light blanket or stuffed animal from age 1, a goodbye party or a trade for a toy, praise, and a sleep plan.

sources.title: Toddler Reading Time (stories)
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Kandia N. Lewis, PhD, August 2023)
sources.quote: Between the ages of 1 and 3, toddlers have celebrations and challenges. So it can help for them to hear stories about other kids and how they faced their fears about what's under the bed or learned how to use the potty.
sources.supports: Hearing stories about other kids facing a challenge can help a toddler. Said as a general help, not a promise of a result.
